title: Common Core L.CCR.5 Explained
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart explains L.CCR.5 - figurative language, word relationships, and nuance in word meanings - by renaming it the Bradbury standard. The joke has a pedagogical point: because he is required to teach Fahrenheit 451 to freshmen, he already has a text whose first page delivers a serpent that is a hose, venom that is kerosene, and a conductor who is a pyromaniacal fireman. He then makes the more important move, leaving literature to show the same standard operating in journalism, where Leonard Pitts' cluster of related words - crusade, quixotic, undaunted, tilting at windmills - quietly casts a subject as an outmatched knight. That example turns word relationships from an ornamental topic into a tool of argument that students need in order to read nonfiction accurately. He also notes the required CCSS documents are thick with L.CCR.5 tasks, so the standard is not confined to English class. His closing claim is about method rather than content: the practice opportunities exist in almost any text, and the work belongs inside a text being read or written rather than in worksheets and banal exercises.
points: Stuart's Bradbury framing is a staffing argument in disguise: a text already mandated in his building supplies more figurative-language instruction than any standalone unit would.
The Leonard Pitts example is the essay's strongest evidence - a writer's chosen word cluster does argumentative work implicitly, which makes nuance a reading-comprehension issue, not a poetry issue.
He extends the standard past literature to the informational texts the CCSS itself requires, undercutting the assumption that word-play instruction is the English teacher's private business.
The closing rule is the transferable one: teach L.CCR.5 in the context of an actual text being read or written, never through worksheets or decontextualized exercises.
quotes: Ray Bradbury was dominating this standard from the day he was born. In fact, before he passed away, Ray wrote L.CCR.5.
But it is true that Bradbury is one of the greatest language-player-with'ers of all time. He couldn't leave language alone; he compulsively submitted it to the writerly equivalent of hot yoga.

The reason I call this the Bradbury standard is because, as a freshman English teacher in our building, I'm required to teach Fahrenheit 451. Within the first page of that book, readers are faced with a serpent that's actually a hose, venom that's actually kerosene, and an orchestral conductor that's actually a pyromaniacal fireman.

And this is just the figurative language. Throughout the rest of the book, students are repeatedly faced with word nuance (e.g., the use of the word “anti-social”), odd word relationships, and boatloads of similes, metaphors, personifications, hyperboles, allusions…

In this editorial, Pitts uses these words: crusade, quixotic, undaunted, mission, driven, tilting at windmills. Through using these related words, he implicitly paints Robert Kilmer as a hopelessly outmatched but pure-hearted knight of contemporary US politics.

Or consider the several texts that are required by the CCSS. In these documents and text types, there are L.CCR.5 tasks galore. In short, there are chances to practice L.CCR.5 in almost any text you put in front of students; the key is to do this work in the context of an actual text, either one being read or one being written, rather than via worksheets or banal exercises.
